title: Every 911 Call Starts With One Question #shorts
summary: Americans make an estimated 240 million calls to 911 a year (FCC). For cell phones, location rules began with the cell site (1996) and then latitude and longitude within 125 meters.
sources: Consumers make 240 million calls to 911 each year, and in many areas 80% or more are from wireless phones; z-axis (vertical) accuracy of plus or minus 3 meters for 80% of indoor wireless E911 calls, in the top 25 markets by 3 Apr 2021 and the top 50 by 3 Apr 2023; nearly all smartphones appear to have barometric pressure sensors; it is not now technically feasible to reliably convert z-axis data to a floor level and no authoritative floor database exists; dispatchable location = street address, floor level and office or apartment number (FCC Fifth Report and Order, Wireless E911 Location Accuracy Requirements, Federal Register, 16 Jan 2020): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2020-01-16/html/2019-28483.htm

Phase I: relay the caller's number (ANI) and the location of the cell site or base station receiving the 911 call; Phase II: identify the caller's latitude and longitude within 125 meters in 67 percent of cases, within five years of the 1 Oct 1996 effective date (FCC E911 Report and Order, Federal Register, 2 Aug 1996): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1996-08-02/html/96-19662.htm

scenes.narration: Americans make an estimated {240 million|two hundred forty million} calls to {911|nine one one} a year.
Every one starts with one question: where are you?
For cell phones, the first answer came in {1996|nineteen ninety-six}: the cell site that took the call.
Then latitude and longitude, within {125|a hundred twenty-five} meters in {67%|sixty-seven percent} of calls.
